Upālipañcaka 1. Anissitavagga (The Chapter on Not Being Dependent)
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Then the Venerable Upāli approached the Blessed One; having approached and paid homage to the Blessed One, he sat down to one side.
As he was sitting there, the Venerable Upāli said this to the Blessed One:
“Bhante, with how many qualities must a bhikkhu be endowed to live independently for as long as life lasts?
“Upāli, with five qualities must a bhikkhu be endowed to live independently for as long as life lasts.
Which five?”
He does not know the Uposatha; he does not know the Uposatha ritual; he does not know the Pātimokkha; he does not know the recitation of the Pātimokkha; and he has fewer than five years of seniority.
Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with these five factors must live without formal dependence for as long as life lasts.
Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with five factors must live without formal dependence for as long as life lasts.
Which five? He knows the Uposatha; he knows the Uposatha ritual; he knows the Pātimokkha; he knows the recitation of the Pātimokkha; and he has five years of seniority or more.
Possessing these five factors, Upāli, a bhikkhu may live independently for as long as life lasts.
Furthermore, Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with five qualities should live as one who is not dependent for life.

What are the five? He does not know the invitation ceremony; he does not know the formal act of invitation; he does not know the Pātimokkha; he does not know the recitation of the Pātimokkha; and he has fewer than five years of seniority.
"Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with these five factors may live independently for as long as life lasts.
Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with five factors may live independently for as long as life lasts.
Which five?"

“He knows the invitation ceremony (*pavāraṇā*), he knows the formal act of invitation (*pavāraṇākamma*), he knows the *Pātimokkha*, he knows the recitation of the *Pātimokkha*, and he has five years of seniority or more— Upāli,
a bhikkhu endowed with these five qualities may live for as long as life lasts without depending on others. Furthermore, Upāli,
a bhikkhu endowed with another five qualities may live for as long as life lasts without depending on others.”

Which five? He does not know what is an offense and what is not an offense; he does not know what is a light offense and what is a heavy offense; he does not know what is an offense with remainder and what is an offense without remainder; he does not know what is a grave offense and what is a minor offense; he has less than five years of seniority.
Possessing these five factors, Upāli, a bhikkhu must live for as long as life lasts without being independent [of a teacher].
“Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with five qualities may live independently for as long as life lasts.

Which five? He knows what is an offense and what is not an offense; he knows what is a light offense and what is a heavy offense; he knows what is an offense with remainder and what is an offense without remainder; he knows what is a grave offense and what is a minor offense; and he has five years of seniority or more.
“Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with these five qualities may live independently for as long as life lasts.
“Venerable sir, with how many qualities should a bhikkhu be endowed so that he should not grant full ordination, nor give dependence, nor have a novice attend upon him?
“Upāli, with five qualities a bhikkhu should not grant full ordination, nor give dependence, nor have a novice attend upon him.”
Which five?
He is not capable of attending to, or having someone attend to, a pupil or co-resident who is ill;
nor of sending away, or having someone send away, one who is discontented; nor of removing, in accordance with the Dhamma, anxiety that has arisen.

“Upāli, a monk endowed with these five qualities should not grant full ordination, should not give formal support (nissaya), and should not have a novice attend upon him: one who is unable to train [others] in the Abhidhamma, and one who is unable to train [others] in the Abhivinaya.
Upāli, a monk endowed with five qualities may grant full ordination, may give formal support, and may have a novice attend upon him.”
What are the five?
He is capable of attending to or having his pupil or co-resident attended to when they are ill;
of sending away or having sent away one who is discontented; and of removing, in accordance with the Dhamma, any anxiety that has arisen.

"Upāli, a monk endowed with these five qualities may grant full ordination, may give dependence, and may have a novice attend upon him: he must be able to train [others] in the Abhidhamma and to train them in the Abhivinaya.
Furthermore, Upāli, a monk endowed with another five qualities must not grant full ordination, must not give dependence, and must not have a novice attend upon him."
Which five?
He is not capable of training a pupil or a co-resident in the training of proper conduct;
he is not capable of guiding them in the training fundamental to the holy life, nor in higher virtue, nor in higher mind, nor in higher wisdom.
"Upāli, a monk endowed with these five qualities should not grant full ordination, should not give formal support, and should not have a novice attend upon him.
Upāli, a monk endowed with five qualities may grant full ordination, may give formal support, and may have a novice attend upon him.
Which five?"

“He is capable of training a pupil or a co-resident in the training of proper conduct; he is capable of instructing them in the training fundamental to the holy life, in higher virtue, in higher mind, and in higher wisdom.
Upāli, a monk endowed with these five factors may grant full ordination, give formal support, and have a novice attend upon him.
“Venerable sir, with how many factors should a monk be endowed for a formal act (kamma) to be performed against him?”
“Upananda, a legal procedure should be carried out against a bhikkhu who possesses five qualities.
Which five?
He is shameless, he is ignorant, he is undisciplined, he holds wrong view, and he has failed in his livelihood.”
“Upāli, a formal act (kamma) should be performed against a bhikkhu who is endowed with these five factors.
Furthermore, Upāli, a formal act should be performed against a bhikkhu who is endowed with another five factors.
Which five?”

He is failed in virtue regarding higher morality; he is failed in conduct regarding improper behavior; he is failed in view regarding extreme views; he holds wrong view; and he is failed in livelihood.
Upāli, a formal act (kamma) should be performed against a bhikkhu who possesses these five factors.
Furthermore, Upāli, a formal act should be performed against a bhikkhu who possesses another five factors.
Which five?
He is possessed of bodily frivolity, he is possessed of verbal frivolity, he is possessed of both bodily and verbal frivolity, he holds wrong view, and he has failed in his livelihood.
It is for a monk who possesses these five factors, Upāli, that a formal legal act (kamma) should be performed.
Furthermore, Upāli, a legal act should be performed against a bhikkhu who possesses five qualities.
Which five? He is possessed of bodily misconduct; he is possessed of verbal misconduct; he is possessed of both bodily and verbal misconduct; he holds wrong view; and he has failed in his livelihood.
Upāli, a formal act should be performed against a bhikkhu who is endowed with these five qualities.
Furthermore, Upāli, a formal act should be performed against a bhikkhu who is endowed with another five qualities.
What are those five?
He is possessed of bodily harmfulness; he is possessed of verbal harmfulness; he is possessed of both bodily and verbal harmfulness; he holds wrong view;
and he has failed in his livelihood—it is for a monk endowed with these five factors, Upāli, that a formal act (kamma) should be performed.
Furthermore, Upāli, a formal act should be performed against a monk who is endowed with another five factors.
Which five?

He is possessed of wrong livelihood by way of body; he is possessed of wrong livelihood by way of speech; he is possessed of wrong livelihood by way of both body and speech; he holds wrong view; and he has failed in his livelihood.
It is for a monk who is possessed of these five factors, Upāli, that a formal act (kamma) should be performed.
Furthermore, Upāli, a legal act should be performed against a bhikkhu who possesses five qualities.
What are the five?

He has committed an offense and has been subjected to a formal act; he gives full admission; he gives dependence; he keeps a novice; he consents to being appointed as an instructor of bhikkhunīs; and even when appointed, he instructs the bhikkhunīs.
"Upāli, a formal act (kamma) should be performed against a bhikkhu who is endowed with these five qualities.
Furthermore, Upāli, a formal act should be performed against a bhikkhu who is endowed with another five qualities.
Which five?"
If a monk commits the same offense for which the Saṅgha has performed a formal act, or another offense of a similar kind, or one more serious than that;
and if he censures the formal act and censures those who performed it—Upāli, a formal act should be performed against a monk who possesses these five qualities.
Furthermore, Upāli, a formal act should be performed against a monk who possesses another five qualities.
"By which five?
He speaks dispraise of the Buddha, he speaks dispraise of the Dhamma, he speaks dispraise of the Saṅgha, he holds wrong view, and he has failed in his livelihood.
It is for a bhikkhu endowed with these five factors, Upāli, that a formal act (kamma) should be performed."
The first chapter, the Chapter on Independence, is finished.
Its summary verse:
Uposatha, Pavāraṇā, ...
The offense and the sick person;
modesty regarding proper conduct,
and [transgression] through negligence regarding higher virtue.
Improper conduct, harmfulness,
and wrong offenses— whatever offense there may be against the Buddha, [one should confess it].
This is the first section on group inclusion.
2. The Section on Non-Settlement:
“Venerable sir, with how many factors is a monk endowed such that a legal procedure against him should not be settled?”
“Upāli, the legal procedure against a bhikkhu who possesses five qualities should not be lifted.

Which five? He has committed an offense; the legal procedure has been carried out against him; he gives the full admission; he gives formal support; he takes a novice as his attendant; he consents to being appointed as an instructor of bhikkhunīs; and even when appointed, he instructs the bhikkhunīs.”
Upāli, the formal act against a bhikkhu endowed with these five factors must not be suspended.
Furthermore, Upāli, the formal act against a bhikkhu endowed with another five factors must not be suspended.
With which five?
If a monk commits the same offense for which the Saṅgha has performed an act of discipline, or another offense of a similar nature, or one more serious than that;
and if he censures the act and censures those who performed it—Upāli, a monk endowed with these five factors should not have his disciplinary act suspended.
Furthermore, Upāli, a monk endowed with another five factors should not have his disciplinary act suspended.
Which five?
He speaks dispraise of the Buddha, he speaks dispraise of the Dhamma, he speaks dispraise of the Saṅgha, he holds wrong view, and he has failed in his livelihood.
Upāli, for a bhikkhu endowed with these five factors, a legal procedure should not be suspended.
Furthermore, Upāli, a legal procedure against a bhikkhu who possesses five qualities should not be suspended.
What are the five?
He is shameless; he is ignorant; he is undisciplined; he is one who causes oppression; and he is not one who fulfills the training in the proper conducts.
“Upāli, the legal procedure against a bhikkhu who possesses these five factors must not be suspended.
“Bhante, when a bhikkhu who is a warrior should approach the Saṅgha, how many qualities should he establish within himself before approaching the Saṅgha?
“Upāli, when a bhikkhu who is a warrior approaches the Saṅgha, he should approach the Saṅgha having established five qualities within himself.”
Which five? Upāli, a monk who frequents the battlefield, when approaching the Saṅgha, should approach with a humble mind,
with a mind like a dust-sweeper, he should be skilled in [offering] seats, skilled in relinquishing [his own seat], and [he should show respect] toward the elder monks.
One should sit on a seat that is appropriate, not encroaching upon others and not obstructing new bhikkhus from their seats.
One should not engage in various kinds of talk, nor in frivolous chatter. Either one should speak the Dhamma oneself, or request another to do so;
or else, the noble silence should not be disregarded. Upāli, if the Saṅgha is performing formal acts that require unanimity;
In that case, Upāli, if a bhikkhu does not consent, he should nevertheless make his view known and inform the community of the concord. Why is that?
Lest I be at variance with the Saṅgha.
“Upāli, a monk who frequents the battlefront, when approaching the Saṅgha, should approach the Saṅgha having established these five qualities within himself.
“Venerable sir, with how many factors is a monk endowed who, when speaking in the Saṅgha, becomes disliked by many people, displeasing to many people, and disapproved of by many people?
“Upāli, a monk who speaks in the Saṅgha is disliked by many people, displeasing to many people, and disapproved of by many people when he is endowed with five factors.”
Which five?

He is one whose speech is boastful, he is one who prattles dependently, he is not skilled in the sequence of discourse, he does not censure according to the Dhamma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the offense, and he does not cause [the offender] to act according to the Dhamma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the offense.
Possessing these five factors, Upāli, a monk who speaks in the Saṅgha is disliked by many people, displeasing to many people, and disapproved of by many people.

“Upananda, endowed with five qualities, a bhikkhu who speaks on behalf of the Saṅgha is pleasing to many people, agreeable to many people, and liked by many people. What are the five? He does not speak with exaggerated assertions; he does not utter dependent pleas;

he is skilled in the sequence of speech; he reproves in accordance with the Dhamma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the offense; and he causes [the offender] to act in accordance with the Dhamma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the offense.”
"Upāli, a monk endowed with these five qualities, when conducting affairs within the Saṅgha, is pleasing to many people, agreeable to many people, and liked by many people.
Furthermore, Upāli, a monk endowed with another five qualities, when conducting affairs within the Saṅgha, is displeasing to many people, disagreeable to many people, and disliked by many people.
With which five?"
He exalts and he disparages; he grasps what is non-Dhamma and rejects the Dhamma; and he speaks much idle chatter.
Possessing these five factors, Upāli, a bhikkhu who conducts business in the Saṅgha becomes disliked by many people, displeasing to many people, and disapproved of by many people.
Possessing five factors, Upāli, a bhikkhu who conducts business in the Saṅgha becomes liked by many people, pleasing to many people, and approved of by many people.
Which five?
He does not praise excessively, nor does he disparage; he grasps what is in accordance with the Dhamma, he rejects what is contrary to the Dhamma, and he does not engage in much frivolous talk.
It is by possessing these five qualities, Upāli, that a bhikkhu who speaks on behalf of the Saṅgha becomes pleasing to many people, dear to many people, and well-liked by many people.
Furthermore, Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with five qualities who speaks in the Saṅgha becomes disliked by many people, displeasing to many people, and disapproved of by many people.
With which five?
He speaks with arrogance; he speaks after having caused a formal denial of opportunity [to be made]; he does not speak in accordance with the Dhamma and in accordance with the Vinaya...
If a monk, Upāli, reproves according to the offense but does not cause [the offender] to act according to the Dhamma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the offense;

and if he does not declare [his view] according to his own view— endowed with these five factors, Upāli, a monk who speaks in the Saṅgha becomes disliked by many people, displeasing to many people, and disapproved of by many people.
“Upananda, endowed with five qualities, a bhikkhu who speaks on behalf of the Saṅgha is pleasing to many people, agreeable to many people, and liked by many people.
What are the five?
He does not speak impulsively; he speaks after having secured an opportunity; he speaks in accordance with the Dhamma and in accordance with the Vinaya...”

“He is one who reproves according to the offense; he causes [the offender] to act according to the Dhamma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the offense; he declares [his view] according to his own view.
Possessing these five factors, Upāli, a bhikkhu who engages in legal proceedings within the Saṅgha is pleasing to many people, agreeable to many people, and favored by many people.
“Venerable sir, how many benefits are there in mastery of the Vinaya?”
“Upāli, there are these five benefits of mastery in the Vinaya.
What are the five?
One’s own aggregate of virtue is well-guarded and well-protected; one becomes a refuge for those overcome by remorse; [the rest of the benefits follow].”
“He speaks with confidence in the midst of the Saṅgha; he refutes adversaries with reasoned argument in a well-subdued manner;
and he is one who practices for the endurance of the true Dhamma—Upāli, these are the five benefits of mastery in the Vinaya.”
The second chapter, on Non-Subsiding, is finished.
Its summary verse:
Āpanna, yāva, and vaṇṇa.
The shameless one, and by means of battle;
the exalted and the one who causes exaltation,
and by force, through mastery.
The Exposition of the First Set of Pairs. 3.
The Chapter on Conventional Usage:
“Venerable sir, with how many factors should a bhikkhu be endowed so that he should not engage in conventional discourse within the Saṅgha?”
“Upananda, Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with five qualities should not speak in the Saṅgha.

With which five? He does not know the offense; he does not know the origin of the offense; he does not know the application of the offense; he does not know the settlement of the offense; and he is not skilled in the adjudication of the offense.”
"Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with these five factors should not speak in the Saṅgha.
Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with five factors should speak in the Saṅgha.
With which five?"

He knows the offense, he knows the origin of the offense, he knows the preliminary application for the offense, he knows the settlement of the offense, and he is skilled in the adjudication of the offense.
It is by being endowed with these five factors, Upāli, that a bhikkhu may speak in the Saṅgha.
Furthermore, Upāli, a bhikkhu who is endowed with another five factors should not speak in the Saṅgha.

Which five? He does not know the legal issue; he does not know the origin of the legal issue; he does not know the application of the legal issue; he does not know the settlement of the legal issue; and he is not skilled in the adjudication of the legal issue.
Possessing these five factors, Upāli, a bhikkhu should not speak in the Saṅgha.
“Upananda, a bhikkhu endowed with five qualities may speak on behalf of the Saṅgha.

Which five? He knows the legal issue; he knows the origin of the legal issue; he knows the application of the legal issue; he knows the settlement of the legal issue; and he is skilled in the adjudication of the legal issue.”
"Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with these five qualities may speak in the Saṅgha.
Furthermore, Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with another five qualities must not speak in the Saṅgha.
With which five?"
She speaks impulsively; she speaks after having created an opportunity for offense; she does not reprove according to the Dhamma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the offense;
she does not cause [the offender] to act according to the Dhamma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the offense;
she does not declare her view as it truly is.
"Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with these five factors should not speak in the Saṅgha.
Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with five factors should speak in the Saṅgha.
With which five?"
He does not act out of favoritism; he acts after having had the opportunity for formal action granted;

he is one who reproves in accordance with the Dhamma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the offense; he is one who causes [the offender] to undergo [the penalty] in accordance with the Dhamma, in accordance with the Vinaya, and in accordance with the offense; he is one who declares [his view] according to his own view.
It is endowed with these five factors, Upāli, that a bhikkhu may engage in legal discourse within the Saṅgha.
Furthermore, Upāli, a monk endowed with five qualities should not speak in the Saṅgha.

With which five? He does not know what is an offense and what is not an offense; he does not know what is a light offense and what is a heavy offense; he does not know what is an offense with remainder and what is an offense without remainder; he does not know what is a grave offense and what is a minor offense; he does not know what is an offense remediable and what is an offense irremediable.
"Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with these five factors should not speak in the Saṅgha.
Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with five factors should speak in the Saṅgha.
Which five?"

He knows what is an offense and what is not an offense; he knows what is a light offense and what is a heavy offense; he knows what is an offense with remainder and what is an offense without remainder; he knows what is a grave offense and what is a minor offense;
he knows what is an offense remediable and what is an offense irremediable—it is by possessing these five qualities, Upāli, that a bhikkhu may speak in the Saṅgha.
Furthermore, Upāli, a bhikkhu who possesses another five qualities should not speak in the Saṅgha.

Which five? He does not know the action; he does not know the performance of the action; he does not know the basis of the action; he does not know the procedure for the action; he does not know the settlement of the action.
It is with these five factors, Upāli, that a bhikkhu who possesses them should not speak in the Saṅgha.
“Upananda, a bhikkhu endowed with five qualities may speak on behalf of the Saṅgha.

With which five? He knows the formal act; he knows the performance of the formal act; he knows the subject matter of the formal act; he knows the procedure of the formal act; he knows the resolution of the formal act.”
"Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with these five qualities may speak in the Saṅgha.
Furthermore, Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with another five qualities must not speak in the Saṅgha.
With which five?"
"One who does not know the subject matter, does not know the origin, does not know the formal rule, does not know the word-for-word commentary, and does not know the sequence of the discourse— Upāli,
a bhikkhu endowed with these five factors should not speak in the Saṅgha. Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with five factors may speak in the Saṅgha."
Which five?
He knows the basis, he knows the origin, he knows the formulation, he knows the sequence of the words, and he knows the connection of the discourse.
It is with these five factors, Upāli, that a bhikkhu endowed with them may speak in the Saṅgha.
Furthermore, Upāli, a monk endowed with five qualities should not speak in the Saṅgha.
With which five?
He goes to a wrong course through favoritism, he goes to a wrong course through ill will, he goes to a wrong course through delusion, he goes to a wrong course through fear, and he is shameless.
"Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with these five qualities should not speak in the Saṅgha.
Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with five qualities should speak in the Saṅgha.
With which five?
He does not proceed by way of favoritism, he does not proceed by way of ill will, he does not proceed by way of delusion, he does not proceed by way of fear, and he possesses a sense of shame—
it is with these five factors, Upāli, that a monk endowed with them may speak in the Saṅgha. Furthermore, Upāli, a monk endowed with another five factors should not speak in the Saṅgha.
Which five?

He follows a course of bias through desire, he follows a course of bias through hatred, he follows a course of bias through delusion, he follows a course of bias through fear, and he is unskilled in the Vinaya.
Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with these five factors should not speak in the Saṅgha.
“Upananda, a bhikkhu endowed with five qualities may speak on behalf of the Saṅgha.
Which five?

He does not follow a wrong course out of favoritism, he does not follow a wrong course out of hatred, he does not follow a wrong course out of delusion, he does not follow a wrong course out of fear, and he is skilled in the Vinaya.”
"Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with these five qualities may speak in the Saṅgha.
Furthermore, Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with another five qualities should not speak in the Saṅgha.
With which five?"
One who does not know the motion (*ñatti*), does not know the performance of the motion, does not know the proclamation following the motion, does not know the settling by means of the motion,
and does not know the pacification by means of the motion— Upāli, a monk endowed with these five factors should not speak in the Saṅgha.
Upāli, a monk endowed with five factors may speak in the Saṅgha.

Which five? He knows the motion; he knows the making of the motion; he knows the announcement following the motion; he knows the settling by means of the motion; he knows the pacification by means of the motion.
It is with these five factors, Upāli, that a bhikkhu endowed with them may speak in the Saṅgha.
Moreover, Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with five qualities should not speak in the Saṅgha.

With which five? He does not know the Sutta; he does not know what is in accordance with the Sutta; he does not know the Vinaya; he does not know what is in accordance with the Vinaya; and he is not skilled in what is possible and what is impossible.
"Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with these five qualities should not speak in the Saṅgha.
Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with five qualities should speak in the Saṅgha.
With which five?
He knows the Sutta, he knows what is in accordance with the Sutta; he knows the Vinaya, he knows what is in accordance with the Vinaya; and he is skilled in what is possible and what is impossible.
It is, Upāli, when a bhikkhu is endowed with these five qualities that he may speak in the Saṅgha.
Furthermore, Upāli, it is when a bhikkhu is endowed with another five qualities that he should not speak in the Saṅgha.

Which five? He does not know the Dhamma; he does not know what is in accordance with the Dhamma; he does not know the Vinaya; he does not know what is in accordance with the Vinaya; and he is not skilled in what precedes and follows.
It is, Upāli, when a bhikkhu is endowed with these five factors that he should not engage in formal proceedings within the Saṅgha.
"Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with five qualities may speak in the Saṅgha.

Which five? He knows the Dhamma; he knows what is in accordance with the Dhamma; he knows the Vinaya; he knows what is in accordance with the Vinaya; and he is skilled in the sequence of what precedes and what follows."
“Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with these five factors may engage in legal discourse within the Saṅgha.
The third chapter on Legal Discourse is finished.
Its summary verse:
The offense, the legal issue,
knowing the offense by force; the formal act,
the subject matter, and the shameless one.
And one who is unskilled in the formal motion;
one who does not know the Sutta or the Dhamma—
this is the third group-inclusion.
4. The Chapter on the Manifestation of Views.
“Venerable sir, how many unrighteous manifestations of views are there?
“Upāli, there are these five unrighteous manifestations of views.”
Which five?

One makes known one's view regarding what is not an offense; one makes known one's view regarding an offense that does not require confession; one makes known one's view regarding an offense that has been confessed;
one makes known one's view through four or five [monks]; one makes known one's view by mind-to-mind.
These, Upāli, are the five unrighteous disclosures of views.
These, Upāli, are the five righteous disclosures of views.
Which five?
One makes known one’s view regarding an offense; one makes known one’s view regarding an offense that is to be confessed; one makes known one’s view regarding an offense that has not been confessed;
one does not make known one’s view to four or five [people]; one does not make known one’s view through the mind with the mind—these, Upāli, are the five legitimate ways of making known one’s view.
Furthermore, Upāli, there are five other ways of confessing a view that are contrary to the Dhamma.
What are the five?
One confesses a view in the presence of someone belonging to a different community; one confesses a view in the presence of someone standing within a different boundary.
One makes one's view known; one makes one's view known in the presence of one who has not yet been made aware of it;
one makes one's view known through four or five people; one makes one's view known by mind-to-mind—these, Upāli, are the five unrighteous ways of making a view known.
"Upāli, there are these five lawful disclosures of views.
Which five?
One discloses one's view in the presence of a fellow resident; one discloses one's view in the presence of one standing within the same boundary."
One makes one's view known; one makes one's view known in the presence of a regular monk (pakatatta);
one does not make one's view known through four or five people; one does not make one's view known by mind-to-mind—these, Upāli, are the five legitimate ways of making a view known.”
“How many, venerable sir, are the unrighteous acceptances?
“There are these five, Upāli, that are unrighteous acceptances.
Which five?”
What is given by means of the body but not received by means of the body; what is given by means of the body but not received by means of what is connected to the body;

what is given by means of what is connected to the body but not received by means of the body; what is given by means of what is connected to the body but not received by means of what is connected to the body;

Which five? He knows the Dhamma; he knows what is in accordance with the Dhamma; he knows the Vinaya; he knows what is in accordance with the Vinaya; and he is skilled in what precedes and what follows.”
Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with these five qualities may be interrogated.
Furthermore, Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with another five qualities should not be interrogated.
With which five?
"He does not know the basis, he does not know the origin, he does not know the formulation, he does not know the word-for-word commentary,
and he does not know the sequence of the discourse— Upāli, a monk endowed with these five factors should not be interrogated.
Upāli, a monk endowed with five factors should be interrogated."
Which five? He knows the basis, he knows the origin, he knows the formulation, he knows the derivation of the words, and he knows the sequence of the discourse—
endowed with these five factors, Upāli, a bhikkhu should conduct an investigation.
Furthermore, Upāli, a monk endowed with five qualities should not be questioned.

What are the five? He does not know the offense; he does not know the origin of the offense; he does not know the preliminary application of the offense; he does not know the settling of the offense; and he is not skilled in the adjudication of the offense.
"Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with these five factors should not be interrogated.
Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with five factors should be interrogated.
With which five?"

He knows the offense; he knows the origin of the offense; he knows the preliminary application for the offense; he knows the settlement of the offense; and he is skilled in the adjudication of the offense.
Upāli, a monk endowed with these five factors may conduct an investigation.
Furthermore, Upāli, a monk endowed with another five factors should not conduct an investigation.

Which five? He does not know the legal issue; he does not know the origin of the legal issue; he does not know the application of the legal issue; he does not know the settlement of the legal issue; and he is not skilled in the adjudication of the legal issue.
Possessing these five factors, Upāli, a bhikkhu should not be questioned.
“Upananda, a bhikkhu endowed with five qualities should investigate a legal issue.

With which five? He knows the legal issue; he knows the origin of the legal issue; he knows the application of the legal issue; he knows the settlement of the legal issue; and he is skilled in the adjudication of the legal issue.”
“Endowed with these five factors, Upāli, a bhikkhu should be interrogated.
The fifth chapter on Taking Upon Oneself is finished.
Its summary verse:
And when it is pure, at the proper time,
with compassion, and with the opportunity;
the undertaking by oneself, and the legal issue.
Also by means of the subject matter;
the discourse, the teaching, and again the subject matter;
the offense, and by means of the legal issue.
6. The Chapter on Ascetic Practices (Dhutaṅgavagga) “Venerable sir, how many kinds of forest-dwellers are there?
“Upāli, there are these five kinds of forest-dwellers.”
Which five?

One becomes a forest-dweller out of dullness and delusion; one becomes a forest-dweller because of evil desires and being overcome by longing; one becomes a forest-dweller due to madness or mental derangement;
one becomes a forest-dweller thinking, "This is praised by the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddhas"; and furthermore, one becomes a forest-dweller simply out of fewness of wishes.
Relying on contentment alone, relying on effacement alone, relying on seclusion alone, and relying on having only this much need alone,
one becomes a forest-dweller. These, Upāli, are the five kinds of forest-dwellers.”
“How many, venerable sir, are those who subsist on almsfood?
… [as before] … How many, venerable sir, are those who wear rag-robes?
… [as before] … How many, venerable sir, are those who dwell at the foot of a tree? … [as before] …
"How many, Bhante, are those who dwell in charnel grounds? ... [as above] ...
"How many, Bhante, are those who dwell in the open air? ... [as above] ...
"How many, Bhante, are those who possess only the three robes? ... [as above] ...
“How many, Bhante, are those who go on a continuous alms-round?
…pe… “How many, Bhante, are those who remain in a sitting posture?
…pe… “How many, Bhante, are those who accept whatever seat is offered? …pe…
“How many, Bhante, are those who eat at a single sitting?
… “How many, Bhante, are those who refuse food offered after the meal?
… “How many, Bhante, are those who take only what is in their bowl?”
“Upāli, there are these five kinds of those who live on alms in a bowl. Which five?
One lives on alms in a bowl out of dullness and delusion; one lives on alms in a bowl because of evil desires and being overcome by longing; one [lives on alms in a bowl] out of madness...”
One becomes an alms-food eater because of mental derangement; one becomes an alms-food eater because it is praised by the Buddhas and the disciples of the Buddhas;

moreover, it is out of dependence on fewness of wishes, dependence on contentment, dependence on effacement, dependence on seclusion, and dependence on the goal of this very practice that one becomes an alms-food eater.
“These, Upāli, are the five who eat from the alms-bowl.
The sixth chapter on the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga) is finished.
Its summary verse:
Forest-dweller, alms-food eater, Tree-root dweller,
charnel-ground dweller as the fifth;
Clothed in robes from a dust-heap, and possessing only three robes.
The practice of begging from house to house in order,
the practice of sitting at a single seat,
and the practice of not accepting a second alms-bowl after having finished eating.
7. The Chapter on False Speech:
“Venerable sir, how many kinds of false speech are there?
“Upāli, there are these five kinds of false speech.”
Which five?

There is false speech that leads to a *pārājika* offense; there is false speech that leads to a *saṅghādisesa* offense; there is false speech that leads to a *thullaccaya* offense; there is false speech that leads to a *pācittiya* offense; there is false speech that leads to a *dukkaṭa* offense—these, Upāli, are the five kinds of false speech.”
“Bhante, with how many qualities must a bhikkhu be endowed so that when he cancels the Uposatha or the Pavāraṇā in the midst of the Saṅgha,
the Saṅgha may suppress him by saying, ‘Enough, bhikkhu! No quarreling, no strife, no dispute,
no contention,’ and then perform the Uposatha or the Pavāraṇā?”
“Upāli, when a bhikkhu endowed with five qualities cancels the Uposatha or the Pavāraṇā in the midst of the Saṅgha,
the Saṅgha may, having suppressed him by saying, ‘Enough, bhikkhu! No quarreling, no strife, no dispute,
no contention,’ perform the Uposatha or the Pavāraṇā.”
Which five? He is shameless;
he is foolish; he is not one who has entered the order; he speaks with the intention of causing [the monk] to fall away, not with the intention of his restoration.
It is for a monk endowed with these five factors, Upāli, who suspends the Uposatha or the Pavāraṇā in the midst of the Saṅgha—
“Enough, bhikkhu! No quarreling, no strife, no dispute, no contention!”—having thus suppressed him, the Saṅgha should perform the Uposatha or the Pavāraṇā.
Furthermore, Upāli, when a bhikkhu endowed with five other qualities suspends the Uposatha or the Pavāraṇā in the midst of the Saṅgha, [the Saṅgha should act] saying:
“Enough, bhikkhu! No quarreling, no strife, no dispute, no contention!”... [and so forth].”
‘In dispute’: having suppressed him, the Saṅgha should perform the Uposatha or the Pavāraṇā.
By which five?
He is impure in bodily conduct, he is impure in verbal conduct, he is impure in livelihood, he is ignorant and incompetent, and he is a maker of quarrels and a maker of strife.
“Upāli, when a bhikkhu endowed with these five qualities suspends the Uposatha or the Pavāraṇā ceremony in the midst of the Saṅgha,
the Saṅgha may, having suppressed him by saying, ‘Enough, bhikkhu! No quarreling, no strife, no dispute,
no contention,’ perform the Uposatha or the Pavāraṇā.”
“Bhante, with how many qualities must a bhikkhu be endowed so that instruction should not be given to him?
“Upāli, with five qualities a bhikkhu must be endowed so that instruction should not be given to him.
Which five?

“He does not know what is an offense and what is not an offense; he does not know what is a light offense and what is a heavy offense; he does not know what is an offense with remainder and what is an offense without remainder; he does not know what is a grave offense and what is a minor offense; he does not know what is an offense remediable and what is an offense irremediable.
Upāli, an examination should not be granted to a bhikkhu who possesses these five qualities.
Upāli, an examination should be granted to a bhikkhu who possesses five qualities.”

“By which five? He knows what is an offense and what is not an offense; he knows what is a light offense and what is a heavy offense; he knows what is an offense with remainder and what is an offense without remainder; he knows what is a grave offense and what is a minor offense; he knows what is an offense remediable and what is an offense irremediable.
It is by these five qualities, Upāli, that a bhikkhu should be granted formal interrogation.”
“Venerable sir, in how many ways does a bhikkhu incur an offense?
“Upāli, in five ways a bhikkhu incurs an offense.
Which five?”
Lack of shame, lack of knowledge, being overcome by remorse, perceiving what is unallowable as allowable, and perceiving what is allowable as unallowable—
by these five ways, Upāli, a bhikkhu incurs an offense. Furthermore, Upāli,
there are another five ways in which a bhikkhu incurs an offense.
“By which five? By not seeing,
by not hearing, by being asleep, by perceiving it as such [when it was not], and by lapse of mindfulness—
by these five ways, Upāli, a bhikkhu incurs an offense.”
“How many, venerable sir, are the enmities?
“There are these five enmities, Upāli.
Which five?”
“Killing living beings, taking what is not given, sexual misconduct, false speech, and the use of fermented and distilled liquors that cause heedlessness—
these, Upāli, are the five offenses.
“How many, Bhante, are the abstentions?”
“Upāli, there are these five abstentions.
Which five?

Abstinence from taking life, abstinence from taking what is not given, abstinence from sexual misconduct, abstinence from false speech, and abstinence from fermented and distilled liquors and intoxicants which are the basis for negligence.”
“These, Upāli, are the five abstentions.
“How many, Bhante, are the calamities?
“There are these five calamities, Upāli.”
“What are the five?
Loss of relatives, loss of wealth, loss of health, loss of virtue,
and loss of view— these, Upāli, are the five losses.”
“How many, venerable sir, are the accomplishments?
“There are these five accomplishments, Upāli.
Which five?”
“Perfection of kinsmen, perfection of wealth, perfection of health, perfection of virtue,
and perfection of view— these, Upāli, are the five perfections.
The seventh chapter on False Speech is finished.
Its summary verse:
False speech, and oppression,
and further questioning by others;
Offense and [freedom from it] by others,
enmity and also the avoidance of enmity;
misfortune and indeed prosperity.
The seventh chapter on group inclusion.
8. The Chapter on Exhorting the Bhikkhunīs:
“Venerable sir, with how many qualities should a bhikkhu be endowed for the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs to perform a formal act against him?”

“Upananda, Upananda! When a bhikkhu possesses five qualities, a formal act must be performed against him by the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs alone, and that bhikkhu is not to be saluted by the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs.

What are the five? He reveals his body to the bhikkhunīs; he reveals his thigh; he reveals his private parts; he reveals both shoulders; he makes advances; he consorts with householders. When a bhikkhu possesses these five qualities, a formal act must be performed against him by the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs alone, and that bhikkhu is not to be saluted by the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs.”
"Upāli, for a bhikkhu endowed with these five qualities, a formal act must be performed by the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha alone;
that bhikkhu is not to be saluted by the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha.
Furthermore, Upāli, for a bhikkhu endowed with another five qualities, a formal act must be performed by the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha alone; that bhikkhu is not to be saluted by the Bhikkhunī Saṅgha."

Which five? He strives for the non-acquisition of requisites for the bhikkhunīs; he strives for the harm of the bhikkhunīs; he strives for the displacement of the bhikkhunīs; he reviles and abuses the bhikkhunīs; he causes schism between the bhikkhus and the bhikkhunīs.

It is when a bhikkhu possesses these five factors, Upāli, that a formal act (kamma) must be performed against him by the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs alone; that bhikkhu is not to be saluted by the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs.

Furthermore, Upāli, when a bhikkhu possesses five qualities, a formal act must be performed against him by the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs alone, and that bhikkhu is not to be saluted by the Saṅgha of bhikkhunīs.

What are the five? He strives for the non-acquisition of bhikkhunīs; he strives for the harm of bhikkhunīs; he strives for the displacement of bhikkhunīs; he reviles and insults bhikkhunīs; and he brings bhikkhus into association with bhikkhunīs.

“Upāli, when a bhikkhu is endowed with these five factors, a formal act (kamma) must be performed against him by the community of bhikkhunīs alone; that bhikkhu is not to be saluted by the community of bhikkhunīs.
“Venerable sir, how many factors must a bhikkhunī possess for a formal act to be performed against her?
“Upāli, a formal act must be performed against a bhikkhunī who possesses five factors.”
Which five? She reveals her body to the bhikkhus; she reveals her thigh; she reveals her private parts; she reveals both her shoulders; she flashes her light; she associates with householders.
It is when a bhikkhunī is possessed of these five factors, Upāli, that a formal act (kamma) should be performed against her.
Furthermore, Upāli, a legal procedure may be carried out against a bhikkhunī who possesses five qualities.

What are the five? She strives for the non-acquisition of gains by the bhikkhus; she strives for the harm of the bhikkhus; she strives for the removal of the bhikkhus from their residence; she reviles and abuses the bhikkhus; and she causes dissension between the bhikkhunīs and the bhikkhus.
"Upāli, a formal act (kamma) should be performed against a bhikkhunī who possesses these five qualities.
Furthermore, Upāli, a formal act should be performed against a bhikkhunī who possesses another five qualities.
What are those five?"

"She strives for the non-acquisition of gains for the bhikkhus; she strives for the harm of the bhikkhus; she strives for the removal of the bhikkhus from their residence; she reviles and abuses the bhikkhus;
she causes bhikkhunīs to associate with bhikkhus—it is when a bhikkhunī is endowed with these five factors, Upāli, that a formal act (kamma) should be performed against her.
"Venerable sir, how many factors must a bhikkhu possess so that his exhortation of the bhikkhunīs is not to be suspended?"
“Upananda, Upāli, a monk endowed with five qualities should not suspend the exhortation of the bhikkhunīs.

Which five? He is shameless; he is ignorant; he is not one who has attained the goal; he speaks with the intention of causing them to fall away, not with the intention of their emergence; and he does not speak in accordance with the Dhamma. A monk endowed with these five qualities should not suspend the exhortation of the bhikkhunīs.”
"Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with these five qualities should not suspend the exhortation of the bhikkhunīs.
Furthermore, Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with another five qualities should not suspend the exhortation of the bhikkhunīs.
Which five?"
He is one whose bodily conduct is impure, whose verbal conduct is impure, whose livelihood is impure, he is foolish, he is incompetent, and he is not capable of providing an answer when questioned.
Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with these five qualities should not suspend the exhortation of bhikkhunīs.
Furthermore, Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with another five qualities should not suspend the exhortation of bhikkhunīs.
Which five?
He is possessed of improper conduct of body; he is possessed of improper conduct of speech; he is possessed of improper conduct of both body and speech;
he is one who reviles and abuses bhikkhunīs; he [associates] with bhikkhunīs...
He dwells in association with improper association.
Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with these five factors should not suspend the exhortation of the bhikkhunīs.
Furthermore, Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with another five factors should not suspend the exhortation of the bhikkhunīs.
"By which five?
He is shameless, he is foolish, he is not integrated into the Saṅgha, he is a maker of quarrels and a maker of strife, and he does not fulfill the training.
It is by being endowed with these five factors, Upāli, that a bhikkhu should not suspend the exhortation of the bhikkhunīs."
“Bhante, with how many qualities should a bhikkhu be endowed so that his exhortation to the bhikkhunīs is not to be accepted?
“Upāli, with five qualities a bhikkhu should not have his exhortation to the bhikkhunīs accepted.
Which five? [The Buddha then enumerates them.]”
He is possessed of improper conduct of body; he is possessed of improper conduct of speech;
he is possessed of improper conduct of both body and speech; he is one who reviles and insults bhikkhunīs;
he dwells in association with bhikkhunīs in an unbecoming manner of association.
"Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with these five qualities should not accept the exhortation of bhikkhunīs.
Furthermore, Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with another five qualities should not accept the exhortation of bhikkhunīs.
With which five?"
“Upāli, a monk who possesses these five qualities should not accept the exhortation of the nuns: he is shameless, he is foolish, he is untrained, he is about to travel, or he is ill.
With how many qualities, venerable sir, should a monk not engage in discussion?”
“Upananda, one should not engage in discussion with a bhikkhu who possesses five qualities.
Which five?
He does not possess the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training; he does not possess the aggregate of concentration of one beyond training... [and so forth].”

He does not possess the aggregate of morality of one beyond training, he does not possess the aggregate of concentration of one beyond training, he does not possess the aggregate of wisdom of one beyond training,
he does not possess the aggregate of liberation of one beyond training, and he does not possess the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation of one beyond training.
Upāli, one should not engage in discussion with a bhikkhu who possesses these five factors.
“Upananda, a bhikkhu endowed with five qualities may be engaged in discussion with.
What are the five?
He is endowed with the aggregate of virtue of one beyond training; he is endowed with the aggregate of concentration of one beyond training...”
He possesses the aggregate of morality of one beyond training, he possesses the aggregate of concentration of one beyond training, he possesses the aggregate of wisdom of one beyond training,
he possesses the aggregate of liberation of one beyond training, and he possesses the aggregate of the knowledge and vision of liberation of one beyond training.
Upāli, it is with a bhikkhu endowed with these five factors that one may engage in discussion.
Furthermore, Upāli, one should not engage in discussion with a bhikkhu who possesses five qualities.

What are these five? He has not attained the analytical knowledge of meaning; he has not attained the analytical knowledge of phenomena; he has not attained the analytical knowledge of language; he has not attained the analytical knowledge of eloquence; and he does not review his mind as it is liberated.
Upāli, one should not engage in discussion with a monk who possesses these five qualities.
Upāli, one should engage in discussion with a monk who possesses five qualities.
Which five?

“He has attained the analytical knowledge of meaning, he has attained the analytical knowledge of phenomena, he has attained the analytical knowledge of linguistic expression, he has attained the analytical knowledge of perspicuity, and he is one who reviews his mind as it is liberated.
Upāli, a monk endowed with these five factors may engage in discussion together with [another].
The eighth chapter on the exhortation of bhikkhunīs is finished.
Its summary verse:
It must be performed by a bhikkhunī alone;
likewise, two others [must be performed] by others.
For bhikkhunīs there are three formal acts (*kamma*);
two pairs [of cases] are not to be set aside;
two are said not to be undertaken.
And there are two difficulties regarding discussions. 9.
The Chapter on Formal Appointments:
“Venerable sir, with how many factors should a bhikkhu be endowed so that he is not to be appointed to a formal committee?”
“Uppāli, a bhikkhu endowed with five qualities should not be appointed to a committee.
With which five?
He is not skilled in the meaning, he is not skilled in the Dhamma, he is not skilled in grammar, he is not skilled in phrasing, and he is not skilled in what precedes and follows.”
"Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with these five qualities should not be appointed to a committee.
Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with five qualities should be appointed to a committee.
With which five?"
He is skilled in the meaning, skilled in the Dhamma, skilled in language, skilled in phrasing, and skilled in what precedes and follows.
Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with these five qualities may be appointed to a committee.
Furthermore, Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with another five qualities should not be appointed to a committee.

Which five? He is prone to anger and is overcome by anger; he is contemptuous and is overcome by contempt; he is spiteful and is overcome by spite; he is envious and is overcome by envy; he is one who clings to his own views, holding them dogmatically and being difficult to disabuse of them.
It is with these five factors, Upāli, that a bhikkhu endowed with them should not be appointed to a committee.
“Upananda, a bhikkhu endowed with five qualities may be appointed to a committee.
With which five?
He is not prone to anger and is not overcome by anger; he is not contemptuous and is not overcome by contempt; he is not spiteful...”
One who is not overcome by resentment, who is not envious and not overcome by envy, who does not cling to his own views, who does not obstinately grasp them,
and who is ready to relinquish them— a bhikkhu endowed with these five qualities, Upāli, may be appointed to a committee. Furthermore, Upāli,
a bhikkhu endowed with another five qualities should not be appointed to a committee.
Which five?
He is irritable, he becomes resentful, he takes offense, he gives rise to anger, and he is impatient and refuses to accept instruction.
Upāli, a monk endowed with these five qualities should not be appointed to a committee.
“Upananda, a bhikkhu endowed with five qualities may be appointed to a committee.
With which five? He does not become angry; he does not harbor ill will; he does not take sides; he does not give rise to resentment; and he is patient and accepts instruction respectfully.”
"Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with these five qualities may be appointed to a committee.
Furthermore, Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with another five qualities should not be appointed to a committee.
With which five?"
He is one who extends [the discussion] but does not remind; he proceeds after having caused an opportunity for intervention to be made;

he does not charge according to the Dhamma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the offense; he does not cause [the offender] to act according to the Dhamma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the offense;
he does not declare [his view] according to his own view.
“Upāli, a monk endowed with these five qualities should not be appointed to a committee.
Upāli, a monk endowed with five qualities may be appointed to a committee.
With which five?
He is one who reminds, not one who lets slip; he acts after having secured an opportunity;

he is one who reproves according to the Dhamma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the offense; he is one who causes [the offender] to act according to the Dhamma, according to the Vinaya, and according to the offense;
he is one who has declared his view as it truly is—it is with these five qualities, Upāli, that a bhikkhu should be appointed to a committee.
Furthermore, Upāli, a monk endowed with five qualities should not be appointed to a committee.
With which five?
He acts out of favoritism, he acts out of ill will, he acts out of delusion, he acts out of fear, and he is shameless.
"Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with these five factors should not be appointed to a committee.
Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with five factors should be appointed to a committee.
With which five?"
He does not fall under the sway of favoritism, he does not fall under the sway of ill will, he does not fall under the sway of delusion, he does not fall under the sway of fear,
and he possesses a sense of shame— it is with these five qualities, Upāli, that a bhikkhu should be appointed to a committee. Furthermore, Upāli,
a bhikkhu who possesses another five qualities should not be appointed to a committee.
Which five?

He follows a course of bias through desire, he follows a course of bias through hatred, he follows a course of bias through delusion, he follows a course of bias through fear, and he is unskilled in the Vinaya.
Possessing these five factors, Upāli, a monk should not be appointed to a committee of inquiry.
“Upananda, a bhikkhu endowed with five qualities may be appointed to a committee.
With which five?

He does not follow a course of action out of favoritism, he does not follow a course of action out of ill will, he does not follow a course of action out of delusion, he does not follow a course of action out of fear, and he is skilled in the Vinaya.”
“Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with these five factors may be appointed to a committee.
“But, Bhante, endowed with how many factors does a bhikkhu come to be reckoned as a fool?
“Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with five factors comes to be reckoned as a fool.”

Which five? He does not know the Sutta; he does not know what is in accordance with the Sutta; he does not know the Vinaya; he does not know what is in accordance with the Vinaya; and he is not skilled in what is possible and what is impossible.
Possessing these five factors, Upāli, a bhikkhu is reckoned as a fool.
“Upananda, endowed with five qualities, a bhikkhu comes to be reckoned as wise.

With which five? He knows the discourses; he knows what is in accordance with the discourses; he knows the discipline; he knows what is in accordance with the discipline; and he is skilled in what is possible and what is impossible.”
"Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with these five factors is reckoned as wise.
Furthermore, Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with another five factors is reckoned as foolish.
With which five?"
“He does not know the Dhamma; he knows what conforms to the Dhamma; he does not know the Vinaya; he does not know what conforms to the Vinaya;
and he is not skilled in the sequence of what precedes and what follows. Possessing these five factors, Upāli, a bhikkhu is reckoned as a fool.
Possessing five factors, Upāli, a bhikkhu is reckoned as a wise man.”

Which five? He knows the Dhamma; he knows what is in accordance with the Dhamma; he knows the Vinaya; he knows what is in accordance with the Vinaya; and he is skilled in the sequence of what precedes and what follows.
Endowed with these five factors, Upāli, a bhikkhu comes to be reckoned as wise.
Furthermore, Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with five qualities comes to be reckoned as a fool.

With which five? He does not know the subject matter; he does not know the source; he does not know the formulation; he does not know the sequence of the words; and he does not know the connection of the discourse.
"Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with these five factors is reckoned as a fool indeed.
Upāli, a bhikkhu endowed with five factors is reckoned as a wise person indeed.
With which five?"
He knows the subject matter, he knows the source, he knows the formal rule, he knows the word-for-word commentary, and he knows the sequence of the discourse—
endowed with these five factors, Upāli, a bhikkhu is reckoned as wise.
Furthermore, Upāli, endowed with another five factors, a bhikkhu is reckoned as foolish.

Which five? He does not know the offense; he does not know the origin of the offense; he does not know the preliminary action of the offense; he does not know the settlement of the offense; and he is not skilled in the adjudication of the offense.
Possessing these five factors, Upāli, a bhikkhu is reckoned as a fool.

Going on alms-round without being invited; going on alms-round without having formally undertaken the practice; eating in a group; possessing robes as much as one requires; and whatever robe-material arises there shall belong to them.”
“Upāli, there are indeed these five benefits in the spreading of the *kaṭhina*.
“But how many, Bhante, are the dangers for one who falls asleep unmindful and lacking clear comprehension?
“Upāli, there are these five dangers for one who falls asleep unmindful and lacking clear comprehension.”
Which five? One sleeps poorly, one wakes poorly, one sees evil dreams, deities do not protect one, and one emits semen— these, Upāli,
are the five disadvantages for one who falls asleep unmindful and lacking clear comprehension.
"Upāli, there are these five benefits for one who falls asleep mindful and clearly comprehending.
What are the five? One sleeps happily; one wakes up happily; one does not see evil dreams; deities protect one; and one does not emit semen."
“Upāli, there are indeed these five benefits for one who falls asleep with mindfulness established and clear comprehension.
“How many, Bhante, are those who are not to be saluted?
“Upāli, there are these five who are not to be saluted.”
Which five?

One who has entered among the houses is not to be saluted; one who is on the street is not to be saluted; one whose head is covered is not to be saluted; one who does not pay attention is not to be saluted;
one who is asleep is not to be saluted—these, Upāli, are the five who are not to be saluted.
Furthermore, Upāli, there are five who are not to be saluted.

Which five? One who is drinking gruel is not to be saluted; one at the head of the meal is not to be saluted; one who has turned away [to eat] is not to be saluted; one who is distracted by something else is not to be saluted; and one who is naked is not to be saluted.
"These, Upāli, are the five who are not to be saluted.
Furthermore, Upāli, there are another five who are not to be saluted.
Which five?"
One who is eating is not to be saluted; one who is consuming food is not to be saluted; one who is defecating is not to be saluted; one who is urinating is not to be saluted;
one who has been suspended is not to be saluted—these, Upāli, are the five who are not to be saluted.
Furthermore, Upāli, there are another five who are not to be saluted.
Which five?

One ordained later is not to be saluted by one ordained earlier; one who is not fully ordained is not to be saluted; one of a different communion who is senior but speaks contrary to the Dhamma is not to be saluted; a woman is not to be saluted; a paṇḍaka is not to be saluted.
These, Upāli, are the five who are not to be saluted.
Furthermore, Upāli, there are five who are not to be saluted. Which five? One on probation is not to be saluted;

one deserving to be sent back to the beginning is not to be saluted; one deserving the trial period is not to be saluted; one undergoing the trial period is not to be saluted; and one deserving rehabilitation is not to be saluted.
“These, Upāli, are the five who are not to be saluted.
“How many, Bhante, are those who are to be saluted?
“These five, Upāli, are to be saluted.”
Which five?
One who was ordained earlier is to be saluted by one who was ordained later; one who belongs to a different community and is senior and speaks according to the Dhamma is to be saluted;

a teacher is to be saluted; a preceptor is to be saluted; and in this world with its devas, Māras, and Brahmās, among this generation with its ascetics and brahmins... [it is the Teacher who is to be saluted].
“The Tathāgata, the Arahant, the Perfectly Enlightened One, is to be venerated by the generation consisting of devas and humans.
These, Upāli, are the five who are to be venerated.
“Venerable sir, when a newly ordained bhikkhu is venerating the feet of a more senior bhikkhu, how many qualities should he establish within himself before venerating those feet?”
“Upāli, when a junior monk is bowing at the feet of a senior monk, he should bow after having established five things within himself.
What are the five?
Upāli, when a junior monk is bowing at the feet of a senior monk, he should have his upper robe arranged over one shoulder...”
“Having done so, Upāli, having raised his hands in añjali, and while stroking the feet with both palms, he should pay homage to the feet, establishing both affection and reverence.
When a junior monk pays homage to the feet of a senior monk, Upāli, he should pay homage to the feet after establishing these five qualities within himself.”
The fourteenth chapter, the Section on the Spreading of the Kathina, is finished.
Its summary verse:
The spreading of the Kathina and sleep...
In between, while eating gruel:
before [the meal] and after it has been set aside,
one who is worthy of salutation should be saluted.
The *Upālipañcaka* is finished.
